system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-02-17 07:15:00 to 2187-02-23 16:59:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and SVC syndrome was admitted with worsening symptoms of superior vena cava obstruction, including neck swelling, headache, blurry vision, and nausea. Imaging confirmed patent internal jugular veins, but a diagnostic SVC-IVC venogram revealed persistent SVC obstruction. An attempted stent placement was unsuccessful, and cardiothoracic surgery was consulted for future bypass planning. A blood culture showed coagulase-negative staph and Enterococcus faecium, but antibiotics were discontinued as the result was deemed a contaminant. Abdominal imaging indicated ileus related to a Crohn’s flare, managed conservatively. The patient improved symptomatically and was discharged home with a plan for outpatient surgical evaluation, medication adjustments, and follow-up.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is an unfortunate woman with long history of Crohns 
disease, fibromyalgia, short gut syndrome, and many central 
lines, ultimately resulting in widespread venous thromboses and 
superior vena cava syndrome manifesting as severe facial and 
shoulder swelling, nausea, and headaches.  She had an attempted 
venogram during her last hospitalization, which was aborted 
because the SVC stenosis was too tight.  Thus, she went to the 
operating room on ___ with the vascular and cardiothoracic 
surgery services for a open SVC/ R subclavian thrombectomy and 
patch angioplasty.  The procedure was uncomplicated.  PLease see 
operative reports dictated by Drs. ___ for 
details of the operation.  

Postoperatively, she was extubated successfully and transferred 
to the ICU.  Her pain and anxiety were well controlled with IV 
medications via a femoral venous line.  Due to a history of 
HITT, she was started on therapeutic fondaparinux on POD0.  She 
was also started on IV lopressor for hypertension, which was 
converted to POs once she was tolerating a diet.  She was 
advanced to regular diet and was transferred to the VICU on 
postoperative day two.  She became somewhat anemic and was 
transfused a unit of RBC for a Hct of 23.  However, as the 
infusion was running, she began complaining of severe LLQ 
abdominal pain.  Her gastroenterologist ___ was called, 
and recommended an abdominal CT scan to evaluate her bowel and 
her left sided groin line.  The CT scan revealed extravasation 
of IV contrast from the groin line and a small hematoma in the 
subcutaneous tissues.  Thus her left groin line was pulled.  
Chronic pain service was consulted to assist in PO pain 
management, and recommended morphine elixer, which actually 
controlled her pain relatively well.  She was also restarted on 
valium, benadryl, and phenergan PRN.

Her hematocrit continued to trend down slowly, to a low of 21.5 
on POD 5.  She also had some bowel movements that were 
reportedly mixed with blood, and did have guaiac positive 
stools.  Cdif toxin was found to be negative.  As she did not 
have IV access, she was given a dose of subcutaeous Epogen and 
oral lasix.  Her hematocrit was found to be 26.5 at the time of 
discharge.  She was evaluated by physical therapy, who 
determined that she was safe for discharge home.  She will be 
discharged with 6 days worth of her current pain/anxiety 
medications, which are working pretty well for her.  A followup 
appointment has been made with her PCP ___ 4 days to assess her 
need for further pain medications, and check her hematocrit.

HISTORY:  ___ woman, status post subclavian bypass.  Assess for lines
and/or pneumothorax.

SINGLE PORTABLE SEMI-UPRIGHT CHEST RADIOGRAPH:  The patient is mildly rotated
to the right.  New clips are noted at the right supraclavicular region.  New
sternotomy wires are intact.  The endotracheal tube terminates approximately
2.0 cm above the carina.  The nasogastric tube is seen traversing through the
stomach.  There are two chest tubes in the medial right apex, and a third in
the medial left lung base.  

The lung volumes are low.  Mildly prominent pulmonary vasculature suggests
mild fluid overload.  There is no pneumothorax or pleural effusion. 
Persistent right apical opacity is more prominent in the current study,
probably rotational artifacts and/or post-surgical.  Small amount of
subcutaneous gas in the right lateral neck is in keeping with recent surgery.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No pneumothorax or pleural effusion.  Endotracheal tube terminates 2.0 cm
above the carina.  Chest tubes as described above.
3.  Right apical opacity more prominent, could be atelectasis, artefactual or
post-surgical.  Recommend repeating chest radiograph with true frontal view to
re-assess.

SINGLE AP PORTABLE VIEW OF THE CHEST

REASON FOR EXAM:  Status post SVC reconstruction, status post chest tube
removal, assess for pneumothorax.

Comparison is made with prior study performed a day earlier.

There is no pneumothorax.  If any, there is a small right pleural effusion. 
Cardiac size is top normal.  Sternal wires are aligned.  Right upper lobe
opacity has improved, consistent with improving atelectasis.  Vascular
congestion has resolved.

AP CHEST 10:15 P.M. ___  

HISTORY:  Brachiocephalic vein repair.  Fever.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Right upper paratracheal region of the mediastinum and the apical pleural
margin are both slightly wider today than on ___ at 9:20 a.m.  Whether this
is the expected post-operative appearance would depend upon timing of vascular
reconstruction, not noted in the request.  Therefore some upper mediastinal
bleeding should be considered.  There is also new consolidation in the right
upper lobe marginating the major fissure, could be atelectasis or developing
pneumonia.  Small right pleural effusion is new.  There is no pulmonary edema.
Heart size is normal.  Dr. ___ was paged to report these findings at the
time of dictation.

HISTORY:  ___ woman status post bypass with abdominal distention.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal x-ray from ___.

FINDINGS:  Four images of the abdomen are obtained, two supine and two
lateral.  There is a mild dilation of the small bowel throughout, all less
than 6 cm.  The osseous structures are normal.  There is a catheter projecting
over the left hemipelvis.  Sternal wires are seen.  There is no free air
noted.

IMPRESSION:  Borderline distention of the bowel loops may represent ileus.

INDICATION:  Evaluate L groin line; evaluate for abdominal pain and
distention.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  5-mm axial sections were taken from the base of the lungs to the
pelvis.  Sagittal and coronal reformats were obtained.  Oral contrast was
given.  120 cc of Optiray IV contrast was pushed by hand through the left
groin line.

FINDINGS:  Limited evaluation of the base of the lungs shows moderate
bilateral effusions with associated atelectasis.  There was no pneumonia or
evidence of interstitial pulmonary edema.  There is a new small-to-moderate
pericardial effusion which is likely hemorrhagic based on Hounsfield units. It
is slightly more dense than simple fluid.  This is likely an expected
postoperative change after sternotomy.  The sternotomy wire borders appear to
be overlapping in the sternum.  There is a small amount of air in the
subcutaneous soft tissue anterior to the sternum.

The liver is unremarkable.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.  The
spleen, adrenals, kidneys and pancreas all are unremarkable.  The small bowel
is not distended.  The large bowel is also not distended without evidence of
obstruction.  At its largest diameter it measures 5.8 cm with normal being up
to 6 cm.  There is no free air in the abdomen.  No lymphadenopathy is noted.

There is active contrast extravasation into the left perivascular space. There
is a probable hematoma medial to this contrast extravasation.  This is
displacing the urinary bladder slightly to the right.  A Foley catheter is
seen in the bladder.

There are no abnormalities or lesions seen in the bone.  There are multiple
subcutaneous calcifications consistent with injection granulomas.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Contrast accumulation into perivascular space secondary to malposition of
the femoral central line.  An adjacent hematoma is present in the
preperitoneal space.
2.  New pericardial effusion, likely with hemorrhagic component.  These are
probably normal postoperative changes.
3.  Bilateral pleural effusions with associated atelectasis.
4.  No evidence of small bowel obstruction or ileus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team doctors. I understand you’ve been having facial swelling, headaches, and nausea again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse over the last few days. Especially when I lie back or lift my arms. My neck feels so tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds consistent with your SVC syndrome. Your last procedure didn’t fully resolve the narrowing in your superior vena cava, and we think it’s gotten tighter again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Last time they couldn’t place the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the blockage was too tight for a stent, we’ve scheduled you for surgery today. We’ll open the SVC and use a patch to widen it, along with removing the clot in your right subclavian vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? That sounds serious. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a major procedure, but necessary. The vascular and cardiothoracic teams will be working together. We’ve reviewed your history, including your HIT, so we’ll use fondaparinux instead of heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I trust you. I just want this swelling to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, it’s Dr. Lee again. The surgery went well. You had a SVC endarterectomy and a bovine pericardial patch placed. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… I feel groggy, but my head doesn’t hurt as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ve extubated you, and you’re on a ventilator no longer. We’re watching your vitals closely in the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you in the ICU for a few days, then move you to the VICU. You’ll start on fondaparinux for blood thinning and metoprolol for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumothorax, and your chest tubes were removed. The right upper lobe opacity is improving—likely atelectasis from surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m breathing easier. But I feel a little anxious being in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve restarted your diazepam and benadryl for anxiety. The chronic pain team also recommended morphine elixir—it’s helping with your comfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw your X-ray. There’s a small pleural effusion and some mediastinal widening. It could be post-op changes, but we’re watching closely for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It’s common after this type of surgery. We’ll repeat imaging if needed. Your blood cultures were negative—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows mild distention. Could be ileus, but we’re not concerned yet. You’re still tolerating food okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been bloated, but I’m eating. I did have some blood in my stool yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your C. diff test was negative, so it’s likely from your Crohn’s. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan because you had pain in your left groin. It showed contrast leaking from your line and a small hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—does that mean it has to come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we removed the line. You don’t need it anymore, and it’s safer to avoid further bleeding. The hematoma is small and should absorb on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My pain’s better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped a bit during the transfusion yesterday. You had a reaction—severe left lower quadrant pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sharp pain. But it went away after they stopped the transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it was related to the line issue, not the blood itself. You’re now anemic, so we gave you Epogen under the skin and oral lasix to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your levels are stabilizing. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your hemoglobin is up to 26.5%. You’re doing well. Physical therapy saw you and says you can walk independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll discharge you with pain and anxiety meds, fondaparinux, and a follow-up with your PCP in four days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about driving or lifting. My sternum feels tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow sternal precautions for 10 weeks—no lifting over 10 pounds, no pushing or pulling. And no driving for at least four weeks, especially on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about showering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower—just let water run over the incision. No baths for six weeks. Call us if you see redness, drainage, fever, or sudden swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. Your facial swelling is much improved, and you’re tolerating a regular diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Here’s your discharge medication list. Fondaparinux daily, metoprolol twice a day, morphine for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine elixir has helped a lot. Can I keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. But your PCP will reassess in four days. We’ve also added ranitidine for stomach protection and docusate for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Crohn’s symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing that conservatively. Continue your usual meds. If diarrhea or bleeding worsens, call your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel anxious at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the diazepam or diphenhydramine as prescribed. And don’t hesitate to call if anything feels off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I watch for blood in my stool again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Occasional blood can happen with Crohn’s, but if it’s heavy or persistent, get it checked. Your recent guaiac-positive stools weren’t from a serious bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, wear your surgical bra and avoid sleeping on your stomach. It helps protect your sternum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend. We’re discharging you in good condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Just glad this is behind me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, follow the instructions, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re all set to go home with home services for support.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and SVC syndrome was admitted with worsening facial and neck swelling, headaches, nausea, and blurred vision due to recurrent superior vena cava obstruction. An open SVC reconstruction with bovine pericardial patch and endarterectomy was performed successfully. Postoperatively, she developed a hematoma at the left groin line site requiring removal, and experienced a drop in hemoglobin requiring transfusion and subsequent Epogen administration. Her pain and anxiety were managed with morphine elixir, benzodiazepines, and antihistamines. She improved steadily, was ambulating independently, and was discharged home in good condition with sternal precautions, anticoagulation, and follow-up planned with her PCP in four days.
